Part 1 of 7

Jefferson in Office

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Summarize the major domestic political developments that took place during Thomas Jefferson’s administration.

IN MY WORDS: Name two big things that happened inside the United States while Jefferson was president.

Reading AMarbury v. Madison (1803)

In the unanimous ruling, Marshall and the other Supreme Court justices held that Marbury deserved his judgeship. At the same time, however, the Court also ruled that the Federal Judiciary Act of 1789, which had given the Court authority in such proceedings, was unconstitutional, which meant that the Court could issue no order to Madison in the case.

The Marbury decision granted the Supreme Court a power not mentioned in the Constitution: the right of what came to be called judicial review, whereby the Court determines whether acts of Congress (and the presidency) are constitutional. Marshall established that the Supreme Court was the final authority in all constitutional interpretations.

Word help: unanimous = all judges agreed · justices = judges on the Supreme Court · unconstitutional = against the Constitution · judicial review = the Court’s power to decide if a law follows the Constitution · authority = power to decide

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “Jeffersonian Republicanism” (Marbury v. Madison (1803); The Court’s Ruling).

Reading BThe Louisiana Purchase and the Haitian Revolution

The unpredictable Napoléon moved to sell Louisiana because of events in Saint-Domingue (Haiti). The French colony was in the middle of a slave rebellion led by Toussaint L’Ouverture . . . Known as the Haitian Revolution, the rebellion lasted from 1791 to 1804, when Haiti gained its independence and became the first independent Black nation.

On May 2, 1803, the United States agreed to pay $15 million (3¢ an acre) for the entire Louisiana Territory. . . . The arrival of the signed treaty in Washington, D.C., presented President Jefferson with a political dilemma. Nowhere did the Constitution mention the purchase of territory. Was such an action legal?

In the end, Jefferson’s desire to double the size of the republic trumped his concerns about an unconstitutional exercise of executive power.

Word help: rebellion = a fight against those in power · independence = freedom from another country’s rule · dilemma = a hard choice · trumped = beat out · executive power = the president’s power

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “Jeffersonian Republicanism” (Napoléon and the Haitian Revolution; Napoléon’s Decision to Sell) (p. 292).

Reading CThe Lewis and Clark Expedition

On a rainy May morning in 1804, Lewis and Clark’s Corps of Discovery, numbering about thirty “stout” men, set out from Wood River, a village near the former French town of St. Louis. Among the original thirty men was Clark’s enslaved man York, who would make significant contributions on the trip and become the first African American to cross the continent and see the Pacific Ocean. . . . Unsure of where they were going and what or whom they might encounter, they were eager to discover if the Missouri made its way to the Pacific Ocean.

Word help: Corps of Discovery = the name of Lewis and Clark’s group · stout = strong · enslaved = forced to work without freedom · continent = the large landmass of North America · encounter = meet

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “Jeffersonian Republicanism” (The Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–1806)).

Trouble at Sea

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe how foreign events affected the United States during the Jefferson and Madison administrations.

IN MY WORDS: How did the war between Britain and France cause problems for Americans?

Reading DImpressment, the Chesapeake, and the Embargo Act

For American sailors, the danger on the high seas was heightened by the practice of impressment, whereby British warships stopped U.S. vessels, boarded them, and kidnapped sailors they claimed were British citizens. . . . 6,200 American sailors were forced into the British navy between 1803 and 1811.

The crisis boiled over in June 1807, when the British warship HMS Leopard stopped a smaller U.S. vessel, the Chesapeake, eight miles off the Virginia coast. After the Chesapeake’s captain refused to allow the British to search his ship for English deserters, the Leopard opened fire without warning, killing three Americans and wounding eighteen.

The unprecedented Embargo Act (December 1807) stopped all American exports by prohibiting U.S. ships from sailing to foreign ports in order to “keep our ships and seamen out of harm’s way.” . . . What the embargo did achieve was the destruction of the U.S. economy. With each passing month, the loss of foreign markets sent U.S. exports plummeting from $48 million in 1807 to $9 million a year later.

Word help: impressment = forcing sailors to serve in another navy · vessels = ships · deserters = sailors who ran away from their navy · embargo = a ban on trade · exports = goods sold to other countries · plummeting = falling fast

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “War in the Mediterranean and Europe” (Impressment; The Chesapeake Incident (1807); The Embargo Act (1807)).

Part 3 of 7

The War of 1812

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Explain the primary causes of the American decision to declare war on Great Britain in 1812 and how the conflict played out in different areas of the country.

IN MY WORDS: Why did the United States go to war with Britain in 1812?

Reading ETecumseh and the Battle of Tippecanoe

Chief Tecumseh decided that the fate of the Indigenous Americans depended on their diverse nations being unified. He hoped to create a single alliance powerful enough, with British assistance, to fend off further American expansion.

William Henry Harrison, governor of the Indiana Territory, met with Tecumseh twice and described him as “one of those uncommon geniuses who spring up occasionally to produce revolutions and overturn the established order of things.” Yet in the fall of 1811, Harrison gathered 1,000 troops and advanced on Prophetstown.

What became the Battle of Tippecanoe was a disastrous defeat for the Indigenous people, as Harrison’s troops burned the village and destroyed its supplies. Tecumseh’s Indian Confederacy went up in smoke, and he fled to Canada.

Word help: unified = joined together · alliance = a group that agrees to help each other · fend off = push back · expansion = growing larger · disastrous = terrible · confederacy = a union of nations

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “The War of 1812” (Conflicts with Indigenous Groups).

Source FTecumseh Speaks to Harrison (Primary Source)

In August 1810, the Shawnee leader Tecumseh spoke to William Henry Harrison, governor of the Indiana Territory. Tecumseh demanded that the United States stop buying Indigenous land.

“Brother, since the peace was made, you have killed some of the Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, and Miamis, and you have taken our land . . . and I do not see how we can remain at peace if you continue to do so. . . . Brother, this land that was sold and the goods that were given for it were only done by a few. . . . If you continue to purchase of them it will produce war among the different tribes . . . Brother, . . . take pity on the red people and do what I have requested. If you will not give up the land and do cross the boundary of your present settlement, it will . . . produce great troubles among us.”

Word help: Brother = a polite way to speak to Harrison · Shawnees, Winnebagoes, Delawares, Miamis = Indigenous nations · purchase of them = buy land from those few chiefs · boundary = border line · settlement = where settlers live

Speech of Tecumseh to William Henry Harrison, August 20, 1810. In Norton, Ch. 7, “Jeffersonian Republicanism,” Comparing Perspectives: “Purchase, Peace, and the Struggle for Land Sovereignty.”

Source F. (1) What does Tecumseh say the Americans have done to his people? (2) What does he warn will happen if they keep buying land?

Point of view. Tecumseh says the land was sold “only” by “a few.” Why would he make this point to Harrison? What was he trying to protect?

Reading GWar Hawks and Three Fronts

In the Congress that assembled in late 1811, the most vocal “war hawks” were Henry Clay of Kentucky and John C. Calhoun of South Carolina. . . . In New England and much of New York, however, there was little enthusiasm for war because military conflict threatened to cripple the region’s shipping industry.

For these reasons and more, the War of 1812 was an unusual conflict. It was three wars fought on three fronts. One theater was the Chesapeake Bay along the coast of Maryland and Virginia, including Washington, D.C. The second was in the South—Alabama, Mississippi, and West and East Florida—where American forces led by Andrew Jackson invaded lands owned by the Creek and the Spanish. The third front might be more accurately called the Canadian-American War.

Word help: war hawks = members of Congress who wanted war · vocal = loud · enthusiasm = excitement · cripple = badly hurt · fronts / theater = areas where fighting happens

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “The War of 1812” (War Fever; A Continental War).

Part 4 of 7

Results of the War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Analyze the most significant outcomes of the War of 1812 on the United States, and their importance.

IN MY WORDS: Name one way the War of 1812 changed the United States.

Reading HGhent, New Orleans, and Hartford

In the Treaty of Ghent (1814), the two countries agreed to return each side’s prisoners and restore the previous boundaries.

Because it took six weeks for news of the Treaty of Ghent to reach the United States, fighting continued at the end of 1814. . . . In just twenty-five minutes, the British had lost some 2,100 men in the Battle of New Orleans . . . The surprising American triumph generated a wave of patriotism.

At the convention, the Federalist delegates proposed new constitutional amendments designed to limit Republican (and southern) political power. . . . The episode proved fatal to the Federalist Party, which never recovered from the shame of disloyalty stamped on it by the Hartford Convention.

Word help: treaty = a peace agreement · boundaries = borders · triumph = big win · patriotism = love for one’s country · delegates = people sent to a meeting · fatal = deadly; it ended the party

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “The Aftermath of War” (The Treaty of Ghent (1814); The Battle of New Orleans (1814–1815); The Hartford Convention) (p. 316).

Reading IThe War’s Legacies

Most Americans viewed the war as a glorious triumph. It also propelled the United States toward economic independence, as the interruption of trade with Europe forced America to expand its industrial sector and become more self-sufficient. . . . By the end of the war, there were more than 100 cotton mills in New England and 64 more in Pennsylvania.

The War of 1812 proved devastating to the eastern Indigenous nations, most of which had fought with the British. . . . The British essentially abandoned their Indigenous allies, and none of their former lands were returned to them.

Word help: legacies = results that last a long time · propelled = pushed · industrial sector = factories and manufacturing · self-sufficient = able to make what you need · devastating = very harmful · abandoned = left behind

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 7, “The Aftermath of War” (The War’s Legacies).

Part 5 of 7

Roads, Canals, Rails, and Machines

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 5: Describe how changes in transportation and communications altered the economic landscape during the first half of the nineteenth century.

Core Objective 6: Explain the impact of the Industrial Revolution on the way people worked and lived.

IN MY WORDS: How did new ways to move goods and new machines change how Americans worked?

Reading JThe Market Revolution

During the nineteenth century, however, farm families began producing surplus crops and livestock to sell, for cash, in distant markets. . . . Such large-scale commercial agriculture, the first stage of a market economy, produced boom-and-bust cycles; and was often built upon the backs of enslaved laborers, immigrant workers, and displaced Mexicans.

Thereafter, the use of wood-fired steamboats spread rapidly. By bringing two-way travel to the rivers in the Mississippi Valley, steamboats created a transcontinental market and a commercial agricultural empire that produced much of the nation’s cotton, timber, wheat, corn, cattle, and hogs.

The railroad quickly surpassed other forms of transportation because trains could carry more people and freight farther, faster, and more cheaply.

Word help: surplus = extra · distant = far away · market economy = making goods to sell for money · transcontinental = across the continent · freight = goods carried by boat or train · surpassed = did better than

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 8, “The Market Revolution” (Water Transportation; Railroads) (p. 334).

Reading KThe Erie Canal and the Telegraph System

Canals also sped the market revolution. The Erie Canal in central New York connected the Great Lakes and the Midwest to the Hudson River and New York City. . . . Thousands of laborers built the canal. They were mostly German and Irish immigrants who were paid less than a dollar a day . . . Transporting goods from Buffalo to New York City previously took three weeks; now it took only eight days. The canal also reduced the cost of moving a ton of freight from $100 to $5.

The Pony Express Company, however, lasted only eighteen months. It was driven out of business by the most important advance in communications: the creation of a national electromagnetic telegraph system. Samuel F. B. Morse, its portrait-painter-turned-inventor, sent the first intercity telegraph message from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore, Maryland in May 1844.

Word help: canal = a long waterway dug for boats · laborers = workers · Pony Express = riders who carried mail on horseback · electromagnetic = using electricity · intercity = between cities · communications = ways to send news and messages

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 8, “The Market Revolution” (Water Transportation; Communications).

Reading LMachines and Mills

The Industrial Revolution, centered on the invention of the steam engine, was the most important economic development in human history since the advent of agriculture. Prior to 1800, most products were handmade by skilled artisans.

Completed in 1793, the cotton gin (short for engine) proved to be fifty times more productive than a hand laborer. . . . Slavery expanded accordingly. The number of enslaved people increased from just under 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million on the eve of the American Civil War

In 1847, McCormick reapers were selling so fast that its inventor moved to Chicago and built a manufacturing plant that produced 4,000 machines a year. . . . Using a handheld sickle, a farmer could harvest a half-acre of wheat a day; with a McCormick reaper, two people could cut twelve acres a day.

It soon became the model for mill towns throughout New England, often referred to as the Lowell system. . . . Mill owners preferred women because of their dexterity in operating machines and their willingness to endure the mind-numbing boredom of operating spinning machines and looms for a wage of $2.50 per week—a wage lower than that paid to men for the same work.

Word help: advent = start · artisans = skilled craft workers · productive = able to make more · reaper = a machine that cuts grain · harvest = gather crops · dexterity = skill with the hands · looms = machines that weave cloth

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 8, “Industrial Development” (The Cotton Gin; King Cotton; Farming the Midwest; The Lowell System) (p. 342).

Part 6 of 7

Immigrants and Workers

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 7: Analyze how immigration altered the nation’s population and shaped its politics.

Core Objective 8: Evaluate the impact of the expanding capitalist “market economy” on workers, professionals, and women.

IN MY WORDS: Who came to America in these years, and how did workers and women try to improve their lives?

Reading MThe Irish, the Germans, and the Know-Nothings

In 1845, a fungus destroyed the potato crop and triggered the potato famine. More than a million people died, and almost 2 million more left Ireland, whose total population was only 8 million. . . . It was mostly Irish men who built the canals and railroads, and mostly Irish women who worked as live-in household servants for middle- and upper-class families.

Unlike the Irish, however, the German arrivals included a large number of skilled craftspeople and well-educated professional people . . . Germans settled more often in rural areas.

The flood of immigrants created a backlash among a growing number of “nativists,” people born in the United States who resented the newcomers. . . . The Know-Nothings demanded that immigrants and Roman Catholics be excluded from public office and that the waiting period for naturalization (earning citizenship) be increased from five years to twenty-one. Their battle cry was “America for Americans,”

Word help: fungus = a plant disease · famine = a time with not enough food · rural = in the countryside · backlash = a strong reaction against something · resented = felt angry about · excluded = kept out

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 8, “Immigration” (The Irish; The Germans; Nativism) (p. 355).

Cartoon“Know-Nothings” Political Cartoon (ca. 1850)

This cartoon was drawn around 1850, when many Americans feared new immigrants. Look at the barrels and at what the two men are carrying.

What to look for: “Irish Whiskey” = the barrel stands for Irish immigrants · “Lager Bier” = German beer; the barrel stands for German immigrants · ballot box = the box that holds votes · polls = the place where people vote

“Know-Nothings,” political cartoon, ca. 1850. In Norton, Ch. 8, “Immigration” (Nativism), caption: “KNOW-NOTHINGS.” Primary source.

Cartoon evidence. (1) What are the two men carrying away? (2) What is the crowd doing behind them? (3) What did nativists fear Irish and German immigrants would do to elections?

Reading NUnions and New Professions

In 1834, the National Trades’ Union was formed to organize the citywide trade unions into a stronger national association.

Strikes led by women followed in industrial cities such as New York (1825), Baltimore (1833), and Lowell (1834). But women, as Louise Mitchell of the New York Tailoresses’ Society explained, faced unique obstacles to improving their working conditions. “When we complain to our employers and others, of the inequality of our wages with that of the men’s,” she said, “the excuse is, they [men] have families to support, from which females are exempt.”

The dramatic social changes of the first half of the nineteenth century opened up an array of new professions. . . . During the first half of the nineteenth century, the only professions considered acceptable for women were nursing (often midwifery, the delivery of babies) and teaching. . . . Blackwell, however, had the last laugh when she finished first in her class in 1849, but thereafter the medical school refused to admit any more women.

Word help: trade union = a group of workers who join to get better pay and conditions · strikes = stopping work as a protest · obstacles = things in the way · inequality = not equal · exempt = free from · professions = jobs that need special training

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 8, “Organized Labor and New Professions” (Early Unions; The Rise of the Professions; Women in the Professional Workforce) (p. 359).
